obtained from the P-ACT amplitude limit after imposing the prior
fa≤MPlf_{a}\leq M_{\rm Pl}. This is a prior-dependent ceiling within the adopted
benchmark, rather than a model-independent QCD prediction. It assumes
fI=faf_{I}=f_{a}, a light axion during inflation, negligible classical evolution
of the axion background, 𝒯θ=1\mathcal{T}_{\theta}=1, and Ωa=Ωcdm\Omega_{a}=\Omega_{\rm cdm}. It also
extrapolates the benchmark fa7/6f_{a}^{7/6} abundance law through the crossover
to the low-temperature, approximately constant-mass regime, where that
scaling is no longer accurate.


Relaxing any of these assumptions can shift the numerical ceiling. Examples
include fI>faf_{I}>f_{a}, a non-negligible axion mass during inflation, a
subdominant axion fraction, a nontrivial transfer factor, or an ultraviolet
completion that permits fa>MPlf_{a}>M_{\rm Pl}. Conversely, taking faf_{a} close to
MPlM_{\rm Pl} makes it increasingly difficult to protect the required approximate
PQ symmetry from Planck-suppressed symmetry-violating operators and other
quantum gravity effects [91, 15]. The
appropriate order-of-magnitude summary within this benchmark is therefore
HI≲1010​GeVH_{I}\lesssim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV} in the most permissive corner of the minimal
pre-inflationary scenario [83, 123].


For the representative order-one choice θi=1\theta_{i}=1, the ceiling is
considerably lower,




HI<2.2×107GeV(95%C.L.),H_{I}<2.2\times 10^{7}\,\,\mathrm{GeV}\qquad(95\%~\mathrm{C.L.})\,,

(2.27)


using the least restrictive of the three fixed-nI​I=1n_{II}=1 amplitude limits
in Table 1. This value is only a useful reference point.
Moving toward the hilltop tightens the bound because the abundance becomes
increasingly sensitive to the initial angle, whereas moving to smaller
angles requires a larger faf_{a} to maintain Ωa=Ωcdm\Omega_{a}=\Omega_{\rm cdm}.


The 𝒪​(1010​GeV)\mathcal{O}(10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV}) ceiling is reached only as faf_{a} approaches
the imposed reduced Planck scale prior. At fa=MPlf_{a}=M_{\rm Pl}, the adopted abundance
fit gives θi≃1.88×10−4\theta_{i}\simeq 1.88\times 10^{-4}. Although
𝒢≃2/θi\mathcal{G}\simeq 2/\theta_{i} grows as the angle decreases, the explicit increase
of fI=faf_{I}=f_{a} dominates, yielding the slow net scaling derived below.


In the harmonic large faf_{a} regime, L​(θi)≃1L(\theta_{i})\simeq 1 and θ~i≃θi\widetilde{\theta}_{i}\simeq\theta_{i}. The
Ωa=Ωcdm\Omega_{a}=\Omega_{\rm cdm} abundance condition therefore gives

(2.28)


Combining this result with 𝒢=2/θi\mathcal{G}=2/\theta_{i} and fI=faf_{I}=f_{a} gives

≃2.72×107​GeV​(Ωcdm​h20.12)1/2​(𝒫I​Imax7.51×10−11)1/2​(fa1012​GeV)5/12.\displaystyle\simeq 2.72\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{GeV}\left(\frac{\Omega_{\rm cdm}h^{2}}{0.12}\right)^{1/2}\left(\frac{\mathcal{P}_{II}^{\rm max}}{7.51\times 10^{-11}}\right)^{1/2}\left(\frac{f_{a}}{10^{12}\,\mathrm{GeV}}\right)^{5/12}.

(2.29)


Equation (2.29) is the small-angle asymptote of the benchmark
function in Eq. (2.23). It accurately reproduces the full
benchmark result at large faf_{a} and overestimates it by approximately
17%17\% at fa=1012​GeVf_{a}=10^{12}\,\mathrm{GeV}, where the exact response
𝒢​(θi)\mathcal{G}(\theta_{i}) departs from its harmonic form 2/θi2/\theta_{i}.


The exponent 5/125/12 is itself conditional on extrapolating the adopted
Ωa∝fa7/6\Omega_{a}\propto f_{a}^{7/6} abundance law. In the asymptotic constant-mass
regime, Ωa∝fa3/2\Omega_{a}\propto f_{a}^{3/2} at fixed θi\theta_{i}, so the abundance
condition instead gives θi∝fa−3/4\theta_{i}\propto f_{a}^{-3/4} and hence
HImax∝fa1/4H_{I}^{\rm max}\propto f_{a}^{1/4} [152, 123].
The dependence on faf_{a} is therefore even weaker in that regime.


This weak decay constant dependence is the essential point. Within the
adopted fit, increasing faf_{a} by more than six orders of magnitude, from
1012​GeV10^{12}\,\mathrm{GeV} to the reduced Planck scale, raises the allowed HIH_{I} by fewer
than three orders of magnitude. Thus, even a near Planckian decay constant
does not reconcile the minimal pre-inflationary QCD axion scenario with
conventional high-scale inflation [83, 23].
This is particularly relevant because decay constants
fa∼1015f_{a}\sim 10^{15}–1016​GeV10^{16}\,\mathrm{GeV} commonly arise in string axion
constructions [147, 65]. Evading the conclusion
therefore requires relaxing at least one assumption entering the minimal
bound, as discussed in Sec. 6.

3.4 The hierarchy of potential derivatives


The small tensor amplitude constrains the local slope of the inflaton
potential, while the measured scalar tilt constrains its curvature. Together,
they imply a pronounced hierarchy between the first two dimensionless
derivatives of the potential. This discussion assumes canonical single-field
slow-roll inflation in which the inflaton generates the observed curvature
perturbation. At leading order,





ϵV=MPl22​(V′V)2,ηV=MPl2​V′′V,ns−1=−6​ϵV+2​ηV.\epsilon_{V}=\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{V^{\prime}}{V}\right)^{2},\qquad\eta_{V}=M_{\rm Pl}^{2}\frac{V^{\prime\prime}}{V},\qquad n_{s}-1=-6\epsilon_{V}+2\eta_{V}.

(3.14)


It is convenient to define




λ1≡MPl​V′V,λ2≡MPl2​V′′V,\lambda_{1}\equiv M_{\rm Pl}\frac{V^{\prime}}{V},\qquad\lambda_{2}\equiv M_{\rm Pl}^{2}\frac{V^{\prime\prime}}{V},

(3.15)


so that ϵV=λ12/2\epsilon_{V}=\lambda_{1}^{2}/2 and ηV=λ2\eta_{V}=\lambda_{2}.


Using the observed scalar amplitude, the dimensionless potential slope is




|λ1|=2​ϵV≃HI2​π​MPl​As=1.43×10−8​(HI107​GeV).|\lambda_{1}|=\sqrt{2\epsilon_{V}}\simeq\frac{H_{I}}{2\pi M_{\rm Pl}\sqrt{A_{s}}}=1.43\times 10^{-8}\left(\frac{H_{I}}{10^{7}\,\mathrm{GeV}}\right).

(3.16)


Throughout the axion-compatible region,
ϵV≪|ηV|\epsilon_{V}\ll|\eta_{V}|, so the scalar tilt gives




λ2=ηV≃ns−12.\lambda_{2}=\eta_{V}\simeq\frac{n_{s}-1}{2}.

(3.17)


For example, Planck 2018 gives
ns=0.9649±0.0042n_{s}=0.9649\pm 0.0042, corresponding at leading order to




ηV≃−0.0176±0.0021(Planck 2018),\eta_{V}\simeq-0.0176\pm 0.0021\qquad\text{(Planck 2018)},

(3.18)


while the representative ACT DR6 P-ACT-LB combination gives




ηV≃−0.0129±0.0017(ACT DR6),\eta_{V}\simeq-0.0129\pm 0.0017\qquad\text{(ACT DR6)},

(3.19)


from ns=0.9743±0.0034n_{s}=0.9743\pm 0.0034 [7, 114]. These results use different dataset
combinations and are quoted only to illustrate the range of curvature
preferred by current analyses.


Across the benchmark interval
HI≃107H_{I}\simeq 10^{7}–1010​GeV10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV}, the resulting hierarchy is




ϵV|ηV|∼10−14​–​10−8.\frac{\epsilon_{V}}{|\eta_{V}|}\sim 10^{-14}\text{--}10^{-8}.

(3.20)


The inflaton potential must therefore have an extremely small dimensionless
slope while retaining a negative dimensionless curvature of order 10−210^{-2}.
This hierarchy is shown in Fig. 3.


Figure 3: Hierarchy between the first two dimensionless potential derivatives
in canonical single-field slow-roll inflation. The observed scalar amplitude
fixes |λ1|=|MPl​V′/V||\lambda_{1}|=|M_{\rm Pl}V^{\prime}/V| as a function of HIH_{I}, while the scalar tilt
fixes |λ2|=|MPl2​V′′/V||\lambda_{2}|=|M_{\rm Pl}^{2}V^{\prime\prime}/V| near 10−210^{-2}. The horizontal bands show
representative Planck 2018 and ACT DR6 determinations. The shaded interval
spans the axion-motivated range between the order-one angle benchmark,
HI≃2.2×107​GeVH_{I}\simeq 2.2\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{GeV}, and the prior-dependent fa≤MPlf_{a}\leq M_{\rm Pl} ceiling,
HI≃1.25×1010​GeVH_{I}\simeq 1.25\times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV}.


Maintaining this hierarchy is nontrivial in a generic effective theory.
In the absence of a protective symmetry or other special structure,
Planck-suppressed couplings between the inflaton and the inflationary vacuum
energy can generate a mass correction of order




δ​mϕ2∼VMPl2∼HI2.\delta m_{\phi}^{2}\sim\frac{V}{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}\sim H_{I}^{2}.

(3.21)


Such a correction produces




δ​ηV∼δ​mϕ2​MPl2V∼δ​mϕ23​HI2=𝒪​(1),\delta\eta_{V}\sim\frac{\delta m_{\phi}^{2}M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{V}\sim\frac{\delta m_{\phi}^{2}}{3H_{I}^{2}}=\mathcal{O}(1),

(3.22)


in conflict with the slow-roll requirement
|ηV|≪1|\eta_{V}|\ll 1. This is the usual eta problem, particularly familiar in
supergravity realizations of inflation [46, 53].


Lowering the overall normalization of a potential with fixed shape does not
resolve this problem. Under
V​(ϕ)→c​V​(ϕ)V(\phi)\rightarrow cV(\phi), the quantities VV, V′V^{\prime}, and V′′V^{\prime\prime} scale
together, leaving V′/VV^{\prime}/V, V′′/VV^{\prime\prime}/V, and hence the potential slow-roll
parameters unchanged. A viable low-scale model must therefore possess an
appropriately flat local shape, often protected by a symmetry or produced by
a controlled structure in the potential. Simply rescaling a successful
high-scale potential is insufficient.


The same derivative hierarchy affects the interpretation of the running.
Define




ξV2≡MPl4​V′​V′′′V2,λ3≡MPl3​V′′′V.\xi_{V}^{2}\equiv M_{\rm Pl}^{4}\frac{V^{\prime}V^{\prime\prime\prime}}{V^{2}},\qquad\lambda_{3}\equiv M_{\rm Pl}^{3}\frac{V^{\prime\prime\prime}}{V}.

(3.23)


At leading order [104],




αs≡d​nsd​ln⁡k=16​ϵV​ηV−24​ϵV2−2​ξV2,ξV2=λ1​λ3.\alpha_{s}\equiv\frac{\mathrm{d}n_{s}}{\mathrm{d}\ln k}=16\epsilon_{V}\eta_{V}-24\epsilon_{V}^{2}-2\xi_{V}^{2},\qquad\xi_{V}^{2}=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{3}.

(3.24)


Since ϵV\epsilon_{V} is extremely small throughout the relevant region,




ξV2≃−αs2,λ3≃−αs2​λ1.\xi_{V}^{2}\simeq-\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2},\qquad\lambda_{3}\simeq-\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2\lambda_{1}}.

(3.25)


Because |λ1||\lambda_{1}| is tiny, even a modest nonzero running corresponds to a
large dimensionless third derivative. For illustration,
|αs|∼10−3|\alpha_{s}|\sim 10^{-3} would imply




|ξV2|∼5×10−4,|λ3|∼3.5×104​(107​GeVHI).|\xi_{V}^{2}|\sim 5\times 10^{-4},\qquad|\lambda_{3}|\sim 3.5\times 10^{4}\left(\frac{10^{7}\,\mathrm{GeV}}{H_{I}}\right).

(3.26)


Current measurements remain consistent with negligible running. For example,
the ACT DR6 extended analysis finds αs=0.0062±0.0052\alpha_{s}=0.0062\pm 0.0052 [33].


Low-scale inflation therefore makes the running especially sensitive to
localized structure and higher derivatives of the inflaton potential. A large
value of |λ3||\lambda_{3}| is not by itself inconsistent with slow roll, because
the quantity entering the slow-roll hierarchy is the product
ξV2=λ1​λ3\xi_{V}^{2}=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{3}. It does, however, show that a Taylor expansion
organized solely by the magnitudes of the individual dimensionless
derivatives λn\lambda_{n} need not be well behaved in the low-scale regime. A
viable model must instead realize the required derivative hierarchy through a
symmetry, an approximate inflection point, a plateau, or another controlled
functional structure.
